summary.title: Writing a Bootloader Part 1
summary.one_liner: You learn how to write a 512-byte x86 floppy boot sector in NASM assembly that prints "Hello world!" using the BIOS TTY interrupt, then boot it in QEMU.
takeaways: The BIOS loads the first 512 bytes of a boot media to address 0x7C00 when the last two bytes are 0xAA55.
At boot the CPU runs in 16-bit real mode, so only 16-bit registers are available and code must fit under 512 bytes.
BIOS interrupt 0x10 with ah=0x0e prints a character in TTY mode; lodsb loads each string byte into al in a loop.
Assemble with nasm -f bin, pad to 510 bytes, append the 0xAA55 magic, and test with qemu-system-x86_64 -fda.
summary.summary: This is Part 1 of a series on writing a tiny 32-bit x86 operating system kernel. It explains the boot process: the BIOS loads the first 512-byte sector to 0x7C00 when it ends in 0xAA55, and the CPU starts in 16-bit mode. The author walks through a complete NASM program that loops over a string and prints it with BIOS interrupt 0x10, then shows how to assemble it, inspect it with hexdump, and run it in QEMU as a floppy image. The article uses a floppy disk to avoid file system complexity and points to Part 2 for protected mode.
